beats.intro: Chapter six, lesson two. The nucleus and ribosomes. [[leaf]]A leaf and a cheek look nothing alike. [[cells]]But zoom in, and both are built from eukaryotic cells, with internal membranes that divide the cell into compartments called organelles. [[map]]Here is our map of an animal cell. [[lit]]Today we visit two stops on it: the nucleus, and the ribosomes.
beats.maps: First, let's compare the animal cell with a plant cell. [[same]]Most of the organelles are the same. Both have a nucleus, ribosomes, rough and smooth endoplasmic reticulum, a Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, peroxisomes, and a cytoskeleton. [[plant]]Only the plant cell has a cell wall, a large central vacuole, chloroplasts, and plasmodesmata, the channels through the wall. [[animal]]Only the animal cell, on this map, has a centrosome and lysosomes. Some animal cells also have a flagellum, like a sperm cell. [[go]]Both keep their DNA in a nucleus. So let's go in.
beats.q1: Quick check. Which cell has which part?
beats.nucleus: Now we zoom into the nucleus. [[big]]It is usually the largest organelle, and it holds most of the cell's DNA, and most of its genes. Most, not all, because mitochondria and chloroplasts carry a little DNA of their own. [[env]]The nucleus is wrapped in the nuclear envelope, a double membrane. Each membrane is a lipid bilayer, and together they separate the nucleus from the cytoplasm. [[pore]]The envelope is dotted with nuclear pores. Each pore is lined with a protein structure called a pore complex, and it regulates which molecules go in and out. Remember the messenger RNA leaving in chapter five? This is the gate it used. [[lamina]]Inside the envelope, a net of protein called the nuclear lamina holds the nucleus in shape. [[er]]And as drawn here, the outer membrane runs straight into the rough endoplasmic reticulum.
beats.inside: Inside, the DNA is not floating loose. [[chrom]]It is bundled with proteins, and DNA plus protein is called chromatin. [[chromo]]When a cell is about to divide, the chromatin condenses into thick, separate chromosomes. [[nucleolus]]And in the nucleus there is one dark region, the nucleolus. [[rrna]]Its job is to make {{rRNA|r R N A}}, ribosomal R N A. [[ship]]There, the r R N A joins proteins to build the parts of ribosomes, and those parts leave through the pores.
beats.q2: Quick check. Click the part of the nucleus that makes r R N A.
beats.ribo: Ribosomes are the workbenches that build proteins. [[made]]A ribosome is a particle made of {{rRNA|r R N A}} and protein. [[sub]]It has two pieces, a large subunit, and a small subunit. [[read]]Together they grip a messenger RNA and build a polypeptide, as in chapter five. [[nodna]]Notice that a ribosome reads the messenger copy, not the DNA itself. [[free]]Some ribosomes float free in the cytosol. [[bound]]Others are bound to the outside of the endoplasmic reticulum, or of the nuclear envelope. [[same]]In a micrograph, free and bound ribosomes look the same. What differs is where they sit.
beats.example: Let's put the two stops together. [[dna]]A gene in the nucleus is copied into messenger RNA. [[out]]The messenger leaves through a nuclear pore. [[sub]]Meanwhile, in the nucleolus, {{rRNA|r R N A}} and proteins have been built into ribosome subunits, and those left through the pores too. [[join]]In the cytoplasm, the two subunits clamp onto the messenger. [[free]]If the ribosome floats free, the protein is made in the cytosol, and it works there. [[bound]]If the ribosome sits on the rough endoplasmic reticulum, the protein is mostly bound for a membrane, or for export from the cell. Lesson three follows that road. [[note]]Same ribosome, different place.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Plant and animal cells share almost all their organelles. Plants add a wall, a central vacuole, and chloroplasts. [[w2]]The nucleus holds most of the DNA, inside a double membrane with pores, and a lamina that keeps its shape. [[w3]]DNA with protein is chromatin, and the nucleolus makes {{rRNA|r R N A}}. [[w4]]Ribosomes, made of r R N A and protein, build polypeptides, free in the cytosol or bound to the endoplasmic reticulum. [[end]]Now try the practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That's the end of chapter six, lesson two.
